events/synod-of-emden-1571/summary: Exiled Dutch Reformed congregations meeting at Emden in East Frisia (October 1571) adopted a Presbyterian-synodal order and the Belgic and Heidelberg confessions, laying the foundations of the Dutch Reformed Church.
events/synod-of-emden-1571/causes/1: Refugee churches in Emden, London and the Rhineland
events/synod-of-emden-1571/consequences/: Reformed public church of the Dutch Republic
Framework later confirmed at the Synod of Dort (1618–19)
events/st-bartholomews-day-massacre-1572: Beginning on 24 August 1572, days after the wedding of the Protestant Henry of Navarre, Catholic mobs and royal troops killed Huguenot leaders including Admiral Coligny and thousands of Protestants in Paris and the provinces. Pope Gregory XIII celebrated a Te Deum; Protestant Europe was horrified.
Court factions around Catherine de' Medici
Edict of Nantes (1598) after further war
events/formula-of-concord-1577/summary: German Lutheran theologians led by Jakob Andreae and Martin Chemnitz adopt the Formula of Concord, settling a generation of disputes; Articles V and VI define the distinction of law and gospel and affirm a "third use" of the law for the regenerate. It entered the Book of Concord (1580).
events/formula-of-concord-1577/causes/0: Disputes after Luther’s death (Majoristic, antinomian, synergist, Osiandrian)
events/formula-of-concord-1577/causes/1: Intra-Lutheran controversies after Luther’s death (Gnesio-Lutherans vs Philippists)
events/formula-of-concord-1577/consequen: Rejected the view that original sin is the substance of human nature
events/moscow-patriarchate-1589/summary: Patriarch Jeremias II of Constantinople, visiting Moscow, elevated Metropolitan Job to patriarch, recognised by the other Eastern patriarchs in 1590–93. Russia took fifth place among the Orthodox patriarchates.
events/moscow-patriarchate-1589/causes/0: Russian power and Ottoman-era poverty of the Greek patriarchates
events/moscow-patriarchate-1589/conseque: Russian Orthodox Church as leading Orthodox body
events/union-of-brest-1596/summary: Most Orthodox bishops of the Kyivan metropolia in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth accepted the authority of Rome while keeping their Byzantine liturgy and married clergy. The Ruthenian (today Ukrainian Greek Catholic) Church was born; other Orthodox resisted, leading to long conflict.
events/union-of-brest-1596/consequences/: Eastern Catholic churches of Byzantine rite
events/twenty-six-martyrs-nagasaki-1597/: On Toyotomi Hideyoshi's order, six Franciscans, three Japanese Jesuits and seventeen Japanese laymen, including boys, were crucified at Nagasaki on 5 February 1597. It was the first great blow against Japanese Christianity.
Hideyoshi's suspicion of Spanish colonial ambitions
Prelude to the Tokugawa ban of 1614
events/synod-of-diamper-1599/summary: Archbishop Aleixo de Menezes of Goa convened the St Thomas Christians and imposed Latin practices, condemned 'Nestorian' books (many burned) and severed ties with the Church of the East. Resentment of Latinisation exploded in the Coonan Cross Oath of 1653.
events/ricci-in-beijing-1601/summary: After eighteen years in southern China, the Jesuit Matteo Ricci was permitted to reside in Beijing at the Wanli court. Dressed as a Confucian scholar, he presented Christianity through Chinese classics, maps and science, winning converts such as Xu Guangqi and allowing ancestral rites as civil honours.
events/smyth-se-baptism-1609/title: John Smyth baptises himself and his congregation in Amsterdam
events/smyth-se-baptism-1609/summary: English Separatist exiles led by John Smyth and Thomas Helwys concluded that infant baptism was invalid and that a true church is a gathered fellowship of baptised believers. Smyth baptised himself (a 'se-baptism') and then the rest of the congregation, forming what is usually counted as the first English Baptist church. Helwys led part of the group back to London in 1612, founding the first Baptist congregation on English soil.
events/smyth-se-baptism-1609/causes/0: Separatist conviction that the Church of England was not a true church
events/smyth-se-baptism-1609/causes/1: Reading of the New Testament as teaching baptism of confessing believers only
events/smyth-se-baptism-1609/causes/2: Contact with Waterlander Mennonites in Amsterdam
events/smyth-se-baptism-1609/consequence: Helwys's plea for religious liberty for all, including non-Christians (1612)
Smyth himself later sought union with the Mennonites, doubting his self-baptism
events/rituale-romanum-1614/title: Rituale Romanum sets the rite of exorcism
events/rituale-romanum-1614/summary: Pope Paul V issued the Rituale Romanum, standardising Catholic rites; its section on exorcising the possessed laid down signs of possession and urged caution, and remained in force until 1999.
events/rituale-romanum-1614/consequences: Centralised and regulated Catholic exorcism for nearly four centuries
events/japan-bans-christianity-1614/titl: Tokugawa ban and the Shimabara rebellion
events/japan-bans-christianity-1614/summ: The Tokugawa shogunate banned Christianity in 1614, expelling missionaries and forcing believers to trample images (fumi-e). After the largely Christian Shimabara rebellion was crushed in 1638, Japan closed itself; 'hidden Christians' preserved a secret faith for over two centuries.
events/synod-of-dort-1618/summary: The Dutch Reformed Church, with delegates from Britain, Switzerland and Germany, rejected the five articles of the Remonstrants (followers of Arminius) and affirmed unconditional election, particular redemption, total depravity, irresistible grace and perseverance — later the 'five points of Calvinism'. Remonstrant ministers were deposed.
events/synod-of-dort-1618/longText: After Jacobus Arminius' death in 1609, his followers presented a Remonstrance (1610) teaching conditional election based on foreseen faith, universal atonement, resistible grace and uncertainty about perseverance. The dispute intertwined with Dutch politics: Prince Maurice backed the Counter-Remonstrants against Oldenbarnevelt, who was executed in 1619, while Hugo Grotius was imprisoned. The synod's Canons answered each Remonstrant article, insisting that salvation is wholly God's gracious work while denying that God is the author of sin. Together with the Belgic Confession and Heidelberg Catechism, they form the Three Forms of Unity of continental Reformed churches. Arminians regarded the synod as partisan and its doctrine as making God arbitrary; Arminian theology later flourished through Wesleyan Methodism, while Calvinists see Dort as safeguarding grace.
events/synod-of-dort-1618/consequences/1: Persecution and later toleration of Remonstrants
events/thirty-years-war-1618/summary: Beginning with the Defenestration of Prague, a Bohemian Protestant revolt became a European war involving the empire, Sweden, Denmark, Spain and France. Germany lost perhaps a quarter to a third of its population; Bohemian Protestantism was suppressed after the White Mountain (1620).
events/susenyos-and-the-jesuits-1622/tit: Ethiopian emperor Susenyos converts to Catholicism
events/susenyos-and-the-jesuits-1622/sum: Persuaded by Jesuit Pedro Páez, Emperor Susenyos professed Catholicism (1622) and under Patriarch Afonso Mendes imposed Latin practices. Rebellion and bloodshed forced his abdication in 1632; his son Fasilides expelled the Jesuits and restored Orthodoxy, leaving a lasting Ethiopian suspicion of Western missions.
events/lucaris-confession-1629/title: Cyril Lucaris publishes a Calvinist-leaning confession
events/lucaris-confession-1629/summary: Patriarch Cyril Lucaris of Constantinople, seeking Protestant allies against Jesuit influence, issued a Confession of Faith (Geneva, 1629) with Reformed views on predestination and justification. He was strangled by Ottoman soldiers in 1638, and Orthodox synods (1638, 1642, 1672) condemned the confession.
events/lucaris-confession-1629/causes/0: Catholic–Protestant rivalry in the Ottoman capital
events/lucaris-confession-1629/consequen: Orthodox confessional statements of Mogila and Dositheos
events/massachusetts-bay-1630/summary: John Winthrop led about a thousand Puritans to found Massachusetts Bay as a 'city upon a hill', a godly commonwealth of covenanted congregations. Congregationalist New England produced Harvard (1636), John Eliot's Algonquian Bible (1663) and, later, Jonathan Edwards.
events/trial-of-galileo-1633/summary: After the 1616 decree of the Congregation of the Index declared Copernicanism contrary to Scripture, Galileo’s Dialogue on the Two Chief World Systems (1632) led to his trial by the Roman Inquisition. On 22 June 1633 he was found “vehemently suspect of heresy”, made to abjure heliocentrism and sentenced to house arrest at Arcetri.
events/trial-of-galileo-1633/causes/1: Counter-Reformation emphasis on authoritative interpretation of Scripture (Trent)
events/trial-of-galileo-1633/causes/2: Personal and political tensions with Urban VIII
events/trial-of-galileo-1633/consequence: Became the emblem of a supposed “warfare” of science and religion, a thesis historians now consider oversimplified
Copernican books removed from the Index in 1835
John Paul II acknowledged errors by Galileo’s judges in 1992
events/antinomian-controversy-1637/summa: Anne Hutchinson, John Wheelwright and (initially) John Cotton accuse Massachusetts ministers of preaching a "covenant of works". A synod at Newtown condemns some eighty errors (August 1637); Hutchinson is tried and banished, and many supporters leave for Rhode Island.
events/antinomian-controversy-1637/cause: Puritan debates over assurance and preparation for grace
events/antinomian-controversy-1637/conse: Growth of Rhode Island as a haven for dissenters
events/westminster-assembly-1643/summary: Called by the Long Parliament during the Civil War, 121 divines with Scottish commissioners drafted the Westminster Confession of Faith (1646), Larger and Shorter Catechisms and Directory of Public Worship. Adopted by the Church of Scotland, they became the standards of Presbyterianism worldwide.
events/westminster-assembly-1643/causes/: Solemn League and Covenant with Scotland
events/westminster-assembly-1643/consequ: Later adaptations by Congregationalists and Baptists
events/first-london-confession-1644/titl: First London Confession of the Particular Baptists
events/first-london-confession-1644/summ: Seven Calvinistic ('Particular') Baptist congregations in London issued a joint confession to distinguish themselves from Anabaptists and to show their orthodoxy. Its 1646 revision added that baptism should be by immersion ('dipping'), which these congregations had adopted around 1641–42.
events/first-london-confession-1644/caus: Rise of Calvinistic Baptist congregations out of the Jacob–Lathrop–Jessey Independent church from the 1630s
Accusations linking all Baptists with the Münster rebellion
events/first-london-confession-1644/cons: Defined Particular Baptist identity alongside the Westminster Confession tradition
Prepared the way for the Second London Confession (1677/1689), still used by Reformed Baptists
